citation.title: Design-Based Inference for Spatial Experiments under Unknown Interference

standing_assumptions:
Source: Wang, Samii, Chang and Aronow, 'Design-Based Inference for Spatial Experiments under Unknown Interference', Annals of Applied Statistics (2025), printed pp. 744-768 (main.pdf, 25 pp.), and its Supplement A (supplements/supplement-a.pdf, 40 pp., which holds every proof). 'p. 754 (PDF p. 11)' is a page of the article; 'Supplement A p. 15' is the supplement's own page number (its PDF page has the same number). Quotations are verbatim from the page images; a bracketed remark inside a quotation is not the paper's text.

(S1) Setting [Section 2, pp. 746-747 (PDF pp. 3-4)]. 'Suppose a set of intervention nodes $\mathcal S=\{1,\ldots,N\}$. Each node $i\in\mathcal S$ can be either a point or a collection of points (e.g., a polygon) that resides in a two-dimensional set $\mathcal X$ indexed by $x=(x_1,x_2)$ (e.g., latitude and longitude). An experimental design assigns a binary treatment $Z_i\in\{0,1\}$ to each intervention node. The ordered vector of experimental assignment variables is $\mathbf Z\equiv(Z_1,\ldots,Z_N)$, and the ex post realized assignment from the experiment is given by $\mathbf z\equiv(z_1,\ldots,z_N)\in\{0,1\}^N$. The experimental design fixes the set of possible assignment vectors as well as a probability distribution over that set. Our analysis considers the case of Bernoulli randomization for each $Z_i$, that is, (possibly weighted) coin flips to determine treatment status at each node.' 'Potential outcomes at any point $x\in\mathcal X$ are defined for each value of $\mathbf z$, $(Y_x(\mathbf z))_{\mathbf z\in\{0,1\}^N}$. Given a realized treatment assignment $\mathbf z$, we observe the corresponding potential outcome at $x$, (1) $Y_x=\sum_{\mathbf z\in\{0,1\}^N}Y_x(\mathbf z)I(\mathbf Z=\mathbf z)$, where $I(\cdot)$ is the indicator function and $I(\mathbf Z=\mathbf z)$ takes on the value 1 if the random assignments $\mathbf Z$ realize to be $\mathbf z$ and 0 otherwise.' 'Let $\mathbf Y(\mathbf z)=(Y_x(\mathbf z))_{x\in\mathcal X}$ denote the full set of potential outcomes when $\mathbf Z=\mathbf z$ and $\mathbf Y=(Y_x)_{x\in\mathcal X}$ denote the full set of realized outcomes.' (pp. 747-748) 'For our design-based inference, the only source of stochastic variation is from $\mathbf Z$.' Potential outcomes and (in Section 6.4) confounders are fixed; every expectation, variance and probability is over $\mathbf Z$.

(S2) Circle averages [Section 2, p. 747 (PDF p. 4)]. 'For $i\in\mathcal S$, we define (2) $\mu_i(\mathbf Y(\mathbf z);\Omega_d)=\frac{\int_{x:d_i(x)\in\Omega_d}Y_x(\mathbf z)\,\mathrm d\zeta}{\int_{x:d_i(x)\in\Omega_d}\mathrm d\zeta}$. In the expression above, $d_i(x)$ measures the distance between point $x$ and intervention node $i$. When $i$ is a point located at $x(i)$, $d_i(x)=\gamma(x(i),x)$, where $\gamma(\cdot,\cdot)$ is a well-defined metric (e.g., Euclidean, geodesic, or a least-cost distance) that satisfies the triangular inequality. If $i$ is a collection of points, then $d_i(x)=\min_{x'\in i}\|x'-x\|$, the minimal distance between $x$ and points belonging to $i$. $\Omega_d$ is a set of distance values, and $\zeta$ is a suitable measure on $\mathcal X$. Therefore, $\mu_i(\mathbf Y(\mathbf z);\Omega_d)$ is the average outcome across points whose distance to $i$ falls in $\Omega_d$.' 'If the points in $\mathcal X$ are dense and spaced evenly, then $\Omega_d$ could be a singleton, $\Omega_d=\{d\}$. ... $\Omega_d$ could be a donut, where $\Omega_d=[d-\kappa,d]$ (with $\kappa$ a user-chosen constant dictating the donut's thickness), or a disk, where $\Omega_d=[0,d]$. ... When it does not cause confusion, we write $\mu_i(\mathbf Y(\mathbf z);\Omega_d)$ simply as $\mu_i(\mathbf Y(\mathbf z);d)$. Similarly, the realized circle average for intervention node $i$ at $d$ is (3) $\mu_i(\mathbf Y;d)=\sum_{\mathbf z\in\{0,1\}^N}\mu_i(\mathbf Y(\mathbf z);d)I(\mathbf Z=\mathbf z)$.' The article notes (p. 747) that data 'may come in various formats including raster data or data on a discrete set of points in $\mathcal X$'.

(S3) Marginalized quantities and the AME [Section 3, pp. 748-750 (PDF pp. 5-7)]. 'To define the spatial AME, first rewrite the potential outcome at point $x$ as $Y_x(z_i,\mathbf z_{-i})$, where $\mathbf z_{-i}$ is a vector equaling $\mathbf z$, except that the value for intervention node $i$ is omitted.' '(4) $Y_{ix}(z_i;\eta)=\mathrm E_{\mathbf Z_{-i}}[Y_x(z_i,\mathbf Z_{-i})]=\sum_{\mathbf z_{-i}\in\{0,1\}^{N-1}}Y_x(z_i,\mathbf z_{-i})\Pr(\mathbf Z_{-i}=\mathbf z_{-i};\eta)$, where $\eta$ is an experimental design parameter indexing the distribution of $\mathbf Z$ (i.e., the probability of treatment assignments).' '(5) $\mu_i(z_i;d,\eta)=\mathrm E_{\mathbf Z_{-i}}[\mu_i(\mathbf Y(z_i,\mathbf Z_{-i});d)]=\sum_{\mathbf z_{-i}\in\{0,1\}^{N-1}}\mu_i(\mathbf Y(z_i,\mathbf z_{-i});d)\Pr(\mathbf Z_{-i}=\mathbf z_{-i};\eta)$, where we use $\mathbf Y(z_i,\mathbf z_{-i})$ to denote the vector of potential outcomes over points in $\mathcal X$ that obtain under treatment assignment $(z_i,\mathbf z_{-i})$.' 'Due to linearity of expectation, we also have (6) $\mu_i(z_i;d,\eta)=\frac{\int_{x:d_i(x)\in\Omega_d}Y_{ix}(z_i;\eta)\,\mathrm d\zeta}{\int_{x:d_i(x)\in\Omega_d}\mathrm d\zeta}$.' '(7) $\tau_{ix}(\eta)=Y_{ix}(1;\eta)-Y_{ix}(0;\eta)$.' '(8) $\tau_i(d;\eta)=\mu_i(1;d,\eta)-\mu_i(0;d,\eta)$.' 'Finally, define the average marginalized effect (AME) for distance $d$ by taking the mean over the intervention nodes, (9) $\mathrm{AME}(d;\eta)=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\tau_i(d;\eta)$.' (p. 750) 'our analysis focuses on experimental designs with Bernoulli assignment, in which case the possible assignments consist of the $2^N$ possible vectors that could be obtained from $N$ (possibly differentially weighted) coin flips.'

(S4) Inferential assumptions [Section 4, pp. 751-753 (PDF pp. 8-10)]. 'Our asymptotic analysis considers a sequence of sets indexed by the sample size $N$. The set of intervention nodes is denoted as $\mathcal S_N$ and the set of outcome points $\mathcal X_N$. Note that assumptions below are assumed to hold uniformly for all large sample sizes.' 'C1 (Bernoulli design). $(Z_1,\ldots,Z_N)$ is a vector of independent Bernoulli($p$) draws.' 'C2 (Bounded potential outcomes). $|Y_x(\mathbf z)|<b$ for some finite constant $b$ and all $x\in\mathcal X$ and $\mathbf z\in\{0,1\}^N$.' 'We work with the assumption that the assignment probability, $p$, is constant over intervention nodes and discuss the extension to cases where assignment probabilities vary in Section 6.4 below.' 'Let $I_{ij}(d)$ be an indicator for whether assignment at intervention node $j$ interferes with the $d$-radius circle average at node $i$, (10) $I_{ij}(d)=1$ if $\mu_i(\mathbf Y(\mathbf z);d)\neq\mu_i(\mathbf Y(\mathbf z');d)$ for some $\mathbf z,\mathbf z'\in\{0,1\}^N$ such that $\mathbf z_{-j}=\mathbf z'_{-j}$; $I_{ij}(d)=1$ if $i=j$; $I_{ij}(d)=0$ otherwise. Then, let $s_{ij}(d)$ be an indicator for whether $d$-radius circle averages at $i$ and $j$ are subject to interference from treatment at some common intervention node $\ell$ (which could be $i$, $j$, or some other third intervention node), (11) $s_{ij}(d)=1$ if $I_{i\ell}(d)I_{j\ell}(d)=1$ for some $\ell\in\mathcal S_N$; $s_{ij}(d)=0$ otherwise.' 'Let's denote the distance between two intervention nodes $i$ and $j$ as $d_{ij}$.' Footnote 3: 'As before, under point intervention, $d_{ij}=\gamma(x(i),x(j))$. Under polygon intervention, $d_{ij}=\min_{x\in i,x'\in j}\gamma(x,x')$.' 'C3 (Local interference.). Let $h:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ be a function independent of sample sizes. For each $d$ and all large sample sizes $N$ and all pairs of intervention nodes $i$ and $j$ in $\mathcal S_N$, there exists a constant $h(d)$ such that if $d_{ij}>h(d)$, then $s_{ij}(d)=0$.' 'This assumption hence implies that, for $i$, $j$ with $d_{ij}>h(d)$, $\mu_i(Y(z,\mathbf Z_{-i});d)$ and $\mu_j(Y(z',\mathbf Z_{-j});d)$ are independent of each other over $\mathbf Z$.' 'Define $\mathcal S_N(i;d)\equiv\{j\in\mathcal S_N:d_{ij}\le d\}$, the set of intervention nodes whose distance to node $i$ is less than $d$.' 'C4 (Intervention node spacing). Let $b:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ be a function independent of sample sizes. For each $d$ and all large sample sizes $N$, the sequence of intervention nodes satisfies $\sup_{i\in\mathcal S_N}|\mathcal S_N(i;d)|\le b(d)$.' 'Let's define the neighborhood $\mathcal B(i;d)$ that includes all the nodes whose circle averages at $d$ may interfere with that of node $i$, (12) $\mathcal B_N(i;d)=\{j\in\mathcal S_N:d_{ij}\le h(d)\}$. From C3 we know that $s_{ij}(d)=0$ for $j\notin\mathcal B_N(i;d)$. From C4 we know that $|\mathcal B_N(i;d)|\le b(h(d))$. Define $c_i(d)=|\mathcal B_N(i;d)|$ and $c_N(d)=\max_{i\in\mathcal S_N}c_i(d)$. Conditions C3 and C4 imply the following condition: C4A (Limited local interference with respect to $d$). For each $d$, $c_N(d)=O(1)$.' 'In our analyses below, we suppress the subscripts for asymptotic sequences unless they are needed to add clarity.' Since $d_{ii}=0\le h(d)$, $i\in\mathcal B_N(i;d)$.

(S5) Estimators and variance estimators [Section 5, pp. 754-756 (PDF pp. 11-13)]. '(13) $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}(d)=\frac1{Np}\sum_{i=1}^NZ_i\mu_i(\mathbf Y;d)-\frac1{N(1-p)}\sum_{i=1}^N(1-Z_i)\mu_i(\mathbf Y;d)$.' 'the Hajek estimator replaces them with $N_1=\sum_{i=1}^nZ_i$ and $N_0=N-N_1$, respectively, (16) $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HA}}(d)=\frac1{N_1}\sum_{i=1}^NZ_i\mu_i(\mathbf Y;d)-\frac1{N_0}\sum_{i=1}^N(1-Z_i)\mu_i(\mathbf Y;d)$.' [The upper limit $n$ in $N_1$ is a misprint for $N$: finding P004-N001.] '(18) $\binom{\hat\mu_0(d)}{\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HA}}(d)}=\arg\min_{(\mu_0,\tau)}\sum_{i=1}^N(\mu_i(\mathbf Y;d)-\mu_0-\tau Z_i)^2$.' '(19) $\hat\Sigma_{\mathrm{HAC}}(d)=(\mathbf X'\mathbf X)^{-1}\Big(\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{j=1}^N\mathbf X_i'\mathbf X_j\hat e_i\hat e_jK\big(\frac{d_{ij}}{\tilde d}\big)\Big)(\mathbf X'\mathbf X)^{-1}$, where $\mathbf X=\big(\begin{smallmatrix}1&1&\cdots&1\\Z_1&Z_2&\cdots&Z_N\end{smallmatrix}\big)'\in\mathbb R^{N\times2}$ and $\mathbf X_i$ denotes the $i$th row of the matrix. The $\hat e_i$'s are the residuals from the regression: $\hat e_i=\mu_i(\mathbf Y;d)-\hat\mu_0(d)-\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HA}}(d)Z_i$. $K(\cdot)$ is a kernel function. $\tilde d$ is a cutoff value, and our setup suggests setting it at $\tilde d=h(d)$. The (2,2)-entry of the estimator $\hat\Sigma_{\mathrm{HAC}}(d)$ is our estimator for the variance of $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HA}}(d)$, and we denote it as $\hat{\mathrm V}_{\mathrm{HAC}}(d)$.' 'C5 (Homophily in treatment effects). For each value $d\ge0$, $\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\Big(\big(\tau_i(d;\eta)-\mathrm{AME}(d;\eta)\big)\sum_{j\in\{i\}\cup\mathcal B(i;d)}\big(\tau_j(d;\eta)-\mathrm{AME}(d;\eta)\big)\Big)\ge0$.' Footnote 10: 'Recall that $\tau_i(d;\eta)=\mathrm E_{\mathbf Z_{-i}}[\mu_i(\mathbf Y(1,\mathbf Z_{-i});d)]-\mathrm E_{\mathbf Z_{-i}}[\mu_i(\mathbf Y(0,\mathbf Z_{-i});d)]$.' '(20) $\hat{\mathrm V}_{\mathrm{SAH}}(d)=\frac1{N^2}\sum_{i=1}^N\frac{Z_ic_i(d)\hat e_i^2}{p^2}+\frac1{N^2}\sum_{i=1}^N\frac{(1-Z_i)c_i(d)\hat e_i^2}{(1-p)^2}$.' Footnote 11: 'Recall that $c_i(d)=|\mathcal B_N(i;d)|$.' Footnote 12: '$K(x)=I(x\in[0,1])$.' 'For some $\alpha<1$, let $z_{\frac\alpha2}$ and $z_{1-\frac\alpha2}$ be the $\frac\alpha2$th and $(1-\frac\alpha2)$th quantiles of the standard normal distribution, respectively.' (p. 756) '(21) $\hat\Sigma_{\mathrm{HAC}}(d)=(\mathbf X'\mathbf X)^{-1}\big(\mathbf X'((\hat e\hat e')\circ\mathcal K)\mathbf X\big)(\mathbf X'\mathbf X)^{-1}$, where $\hat e=(\hat e_1,\ldots,\hat e_n)$, $\mathcal K$ is a $n$-by-$n$ symmetric matrix with $\mathcal K_{ij}=K(\frac{d_{ij}}{\tilde d})$, and $\circ$ denotes the pointwise (Hadamard) matrix product. Denote the eigenvalue decomposition of the matrix $\mathcal K$ as $\mathcal K=\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_iv_iv_i'$, where $\{\lambda_i\}_{i=1}^n$ are the eigenvalues and $\{v_i\}_{i=1}^n$ are the eigenvectors. We define $\mathcal K^{\mathrm{PD}}=\sum_{i=1}^n\max\{\lambda_i,0\}v_iv_i'$, and the corresponding positive semidefinite variance estimator (22) $\hat\Sigma^{\mathrm{PD}}_{\mathrm{HAC}}(d)=(\mathbf X'\mathbf X)^{-1}\big(\mathbf X'((\hat e\hat e')\circ\mathcal K^{\mathrm{PD}})\mathbf X\big)(\mathbf X'\mathbf X)^{-1}$.' [Here too $n$ is a misprint for $N$: P004-N001.]

(S6) Conventions of Supplement A [Supplement A p. 1]. 'Without noted otherwise, the expectation is always taken over random assignments $\mathbf Z$.' 'We write $\mathrm E[\mu_i(\mathbf Y(\mathbf Z);d)|Z_i=1]=\mathrm E[\mu_i(\mathbf 1;d)]$ and $\mathrm E[\mu_i(\mathbf Y(\mathbf Z);d)|Z_i=0]=\mathrm E[\mu_i(\mathbf 0;d)]$.' 'We write $\mathrm E[\mu_i(\mathbf Y(\mathbf Z);d)|Z_i=a,Z_j=b]=\mathrm E[\mu_i(\mathbf a_{\mathbf i},\mathbf b_{\mathbf j};d)]$ for $a,b\in\{0,1\}$.' 'We write $\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{j\in\mathcal B(i;d)}$ as $\sum_{i;j\in\mathcal B(i;d)}$.' So, under independent assignment, $\mathrm E[\mu_i(\mathbf a;d)]=\mu_i(a;d,\eta)$ of (5), and an expression such as $\mathrm E[(\mu_i(\mathbf a_{\mathbf i},\mathbf b_{\mathbf j};d)-c)(\mu_j(\mathbf a_{\mathbf i},\mathbf b_{\mathbf j};d)-c')]$ is the conditional expectation of $(\mu_i(\mathbf Y(\mathbf Z);d)-c)(\mu_j(\mathbf Y(\mathbf Z);d)-c')$ given $Z_i=a,Z_j=b$. [Supplement A p. 4, proof of Lemma A.3] 'Further define $\bar\mu^1(d)=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\mathrm E[\mu_i(\mathbf 1;d)]$ and $\bar\mu^0(d)=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\mathrm E[\mu_i(\mathbf 0;d)]$' (written $\bar\mu_1(d),\bar\mu_0(d)$ in Supplement A.5 and Appendix C); hence $\mathrm{AME}(d;\eta)=\bar\mu^1(d)-\bar\mu^0(d)$. [Supplement A p. 10] 'We use $\mathrm{AVar}(\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HA}}(d))$ to denote $\mathrm{Var}(\tau^{\mathrm L}_{\mathrm{HA}}(d))$', the variance of the linearized Hajek estimator $\hat\tau^{\mathrm L}_{\mathrm{HA}}(d)$ of Lemma A.3 (Supplement A p. 4). [Supplement A p. 11] The class '(27) $\hat\tau(\mu_1,\mu_0;d)=\mu_1-\mu_0+\Big(\frac1{Np}\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf Z_i(\mu_i(\mathbf Y;d)-\mu_1)-\frac1{N(1-p)}\sum_{i=1}^n(1-\mathbf Z_i)(\mu_i(\mathbf Y;d)-\mu_0)\Big)$' (upper limits printed $n$; the sums run over the $N$ nodes).

(S7) Observational setting [Section 6.4, p. 758 (PDF p. 15); Supplement A.6, pp. 13-15]. 'we denote a vector of confounder attributes for intervention node $i$ as $O_i$ and make the following independent assignment assumption: C6 (Probablistic Assignment). For all sample sizes $N$: (i) The random assignment variables $\{Z_i\}_{i=1}^N$ are jointly independent. (ii) There exists a treatment probability model $p(\cdot):\mathcal O\to[0,1]$ such that, for each $i\in\mathcal S_N$, (30) $\mathbf{Prob}(Z_i=1)=p(O_i)$. (iii) For an $\epsilon\in(0,\frac12)$ and for all $i\in\mathcal S_N$, $\mathbf{Prob}(Z_i=1)\in(\epsilon,1-\epsilon)$.' Footnote 19 (p. 759): 'Note that the AME is defined by marginalizing over the independently but not identically distributed assignment variables generated by the assignment mechanism.' Supplement A.6 (pp. 13-14): 'C 1. The following properties hold for all sample size $N$ and for all $i\in\mathcal S_N$: (i) (Fixed Dimensionality)The confounder $O_i=(o_{1i},...,o_{ki})'$ is of dimension $k$. (ii) (Bounded Confounders) Confouders are uniformly bounded: there exists a constant $U$ such that $\max_{i\in\mathcal S_N}||O_i||_\infty\le U$. (iii) (Logistic Model) The assignment probabilites follow a logistic model: for all $i\in\mathcal S_N$ there exists a $\theta_0\in\mathbb R^k$ such that $P(Z_i=1)=p(O_i|\theta)=\frac{\exp(O_i'\theta_0)}{1+\exp(O_i'\theta_0)}$ (iv) Compact Parameter Space: $\theta_0\in\Theta_0$ where $\Theta_0\subset\mathbb R^k$ is a compact set. (v) (Nonsingularity) The smallest eigenvalue of $\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^NO_iO_i'$ is uniformly bounded below. (vi) The MLE estimator is used to estimate the coefficient vector $\theta$: $\hat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}}=\arg\max_{\theta\in\Theta_0}\sum_{i=1}^N\big(Z_iO_i'\theta-\log(1+\exp(O_i'\theta))\big)$.' 'We defined the following IPW estimator: $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{IPW}}(d)=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\frac{Z_i}{p(O_i|\hat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}})}\mu_i(\mathbf Y;d)-\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\frac{1-Z_i}{1-p(O_i|\hat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}})}\mu_i(\mathbf Y;d)$. For brevity, we denote $p(O_i|\theta_0)=p_0(O_i)$. We define the following coefficients: $\beta_{1,N}=\Big(\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^Np_0(O_i)(1-p_0(O_i))O_iO_i'\Big)^{-1}\Big(\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\mathrm E[\mu_i(1;d)p_0(O_i)(1-p_0(O_i))O_i]\Big)$, and, $\beta_{0,N}=\Big(\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^Np_0(O_i)(1-p_0(O_i))O_iO_i'\Big)^{-1}\Big(\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\mathrm E[\mu_i(0;d)p_0(O_i)(1-p_0(O_i))O_i]\Big)$.' 'C 2. For all sample size $N$, $\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\big(\tau_i(d;\eta)-(O_i'\beta_{1,N}-O_i'\beta_{0,N})\big)\sum_{j\in\mathcal B(i;d)}\big(\tau_j(d;\eta)-(O_i'\beta_{1,N}-O_i'\beta_{0,N})\big)\ge0$.' (p. 15) '$\hat{\mathrm V}^{\mathrm{obs}}_{\mathrm{HAC}}(d)=(\mathbf X'\mathbf X)^{-1}\Big(\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{j=1}^N\mathbf X_i\mathbf X_j'\hat\epsilon_i\hat\epsilon_j\mathbf 1\{j\in\mathcal B(i;d)\}\Big)(\mathbf X'\mathbf X)^{-1}$, where $\hat\epsilon_i=\frac{N_1}N\frac{Z_i}{p(O_j|\hat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}})}\big(\mu_i(\mathbf Y;d)-O_i'\hat\beta_{1,N}\big)+\frac{N_0}N\frac{1-Z_i}{1-p(O_j|\hat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}})}\big(\mu_i(\mathbf Y;d)-O_i'\hat\beta_{0,N}\big)$', with footnote 9: '$\hat\beta_{1,N}=\Big(\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^Np(O_i|\hat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}})(1-p(O_i|\hat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}}))O_iO_i'\Big)^{-1}\Big(\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\frac{Z_i\mu_i(\mathbf Y;d)}{p(O_i|\hat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}})}p(O_i|\hat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}})(1-p(O_i|\hat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}}))O_i\Big)$ and $\hat\beta_{0,N}=\Big(\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^Np(O_i|\hat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}})(1-p(O_i|\hat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}}))O_iO_i'\Big)^{-1}\Big(\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\frac{(1-Z_i)\mu_i(\mathbf Y;d)}{1-p(O_i|\hat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}})}p(O_i|\hat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}})(1-p(O_i|\hat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}}))O_i\Big)$'; and '$\hat V^{\mathrm{obs}}_{\mathrm{SAH}}(d)=\frac1{N^2}\sum_{i=1}^N\frac{Z_ic_i(d)\hat\epsilon_i^2}{p^2(O_i|\hat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}})}+\frac1{N^2}\sum_{i=1}^N\frac{(1-Z_i)c_i(d)\hat\epsilon_i^2}{(1-p(O_i|\hat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}}))^2}$'.

(S8) Near-epoch dependence [Supplement A, Appendix C, pp. 25-34]. 'Let $\mathcal S_N$ be a set of intervention nodes equipped with a distance metric $\gamma$ that satisfies positivity and the triangle inequality. Let $H_N=\{H_{i,N},i\in\mathcal S_N\}$ and $V_N=\{V_{i,N},i\in\mathcal S_N\}$ be two arbitrary sets of random variables. Define $\mathcal F_i(s)=\sigma(V_{j,N},j\in\mathcal S_n,\gamma(i,j)\le s)$ ... Denote the $L_p$-norm of a random variable as $||X||_p=(E[|X|^p])^{\frac1p}$.' 'Definition 1 ($L_2$-NED). Let $H_N=\{H_{i,N},i\in\mathcal S_N,N\ge1\}$ be a random field with $||H_{i,N}||_2<\infty$. Let $V_N=\{V_{i,N},i\in\mathcal S_N,N\ge1\}$ be a random field, where $|\mathcal S_N|=N$, and let $g_N=\{g_{i,N},i\in\mathcal S_N,N\ge1\}$ be a set of positive constants. Then the random field $H_N$ is said to be $L_2(g_N)$-near-epoch dependent on the random field $V_N$ if, for all $i$, (51) $||H_{i,N}-\mathrm E[H_{i,N}|\mathcal F_{i,N}(s)]||_2\le g_{i,N}\psi(s)$, for a non-increasing sequence $\psi(s)\ge0$ with $\lim_{s\to\infty}\psi(s)=0$. $H_N$ is said to be $L_2$-NED on $V_N$ of size $-\lambda$ if $\psi(s)=O(s^{-\mu})$ for some $\mu>\lambda>0$. Further more, if $\sup_N\sup_{i\in\mathcal S_N}g_{i,N}<\infty$, then $H_N$ is said to be uniformly $L_2$-NED on $V_N$.' 'Let $\mathcal F_i^c(s)=\sigma(V_{j,N},j\in\mathcal S_n,\gamma(i,j)>s)$'. (p. 26) 'We shall inherit C1 and C2. We relax C3 with the following weak-dependence assumption. C 3. For any $d$-circle average outcomes and for all sample sizes, $\{\mu_i(\mathbf Y,d),i\in\mathcal S_N\}$ is uniform $L_2$-NED of size -4 on the random field $\{Z_i,i\in\mathcal S_N\}$.' 'Denote the corresponding NED-coefficient function as $\psi_d():\mathbb R_+\to\mathbb R_+$.' (p. 27) 'C 4. For each radius $s\ge0$ and all large sample sizes $N$, there exists a $C_b>0$ such that $\sup_{i\in\mathcal S_N}|\mathcal B_N(i;s)|\le b(s)$, with $b(s)=C_bs^2$.' [In Appendix C, $\mathcal B_N(i;s)$ is the set of nodes within distance $s$ of $i$.] (p. 32) 'C 5. The kernel function $K:\mathbb R_+\to\mathbb R$ has the following properties: 1. $K(0)=1$. 2. It is supported on $[0,1]$. 3. It is uniformly bounded: there exists a $K_{max}<\infty$ such that $\sup_{x\in\mathbb R_+}|K(x)|<K_{max}$. 4. It is locally Lipschitz at 0: there exists a $\epsilon\in(0,1)$ and a positive constant $C>0$ such that (101) $|K(x)-1|\le C|x|$, for any $x\in[0,\epsilon)$.' Footnote 19: 'This means that $K(x)=0$ for all $x>1$.' '(102) $\hat\epsilon_{i,N}(\mu_1,\mu_0;d)=\frac{\mathbf Z_i}{Np}(\mu_i(\mathbf Y;d)-\mu_1)-\frac{1-\mathbf Z_i}{N(1-p)}(\mu_i(\mathbf Y;d)-\mu_0)$.' '(107) $\hat v_{i,N}(\mu_1,\mu_0;d,b_N)=\sum_{j\in\mathcal B(i;b_N)}\hat\epsilon_{i,N}(\mu_1,\mu_0;d)\hat\epsilon_{j,N}(\mu_1,\mu_0;d)K(\frac{d_{ij}}{b_N})$, and $v_{i,N}(\mu_1,\mu_0;d,b_N)=\mathrm E[\hat v_{i,N}(\mu_1,\mu_0;d,b_N)]$'. (p. 34) 'C 6. Given a kernel function $K$ and a sequence of bandwidth $\{b_N\}_{N=1}^\infty$, (122) $\liminf_N\Big(\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{j=1}^NK(\frac{d_{ij}}{b_N})(\tau_i(d)-\mathrm{AME}(d;\eta))(\tau_j(d)-\mathrm{AME}(d;\eta))\Big)\ge0$.' Footnote 20: 'Note if $b_N$ is fixed and $K$ is the uniform kernel, this reduces to C5.'

(S9) Label collisions (a reader's note, not the paper's text). Supplement A reuses the labels of the article for different statements: 'C 1' and 'C 2' of Supplement A.6 are the logistic-model block and a homophily condition of (S7), not C1 and C2 of (S4); 'C 3' to 'C 6' of Appendix C are the conditions of (S8), not C3-C6 of (S4), (S5) and (S7); and Supplement A has its own Propositions 1-6 (A.4.1 Proposition 1, A.4.2 Proposition 2, A.5 Proposition 3, A.6 Proposition 4, Appendix C Propositions 5 and 6), distinct from Propositions 1-4 of the article. canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 6.4, the observational Horvitz-Thompson estimator $\hat\tau^{\mathrm{obs}}_{\mathrm{HT}}(d)$ and its unbiasedness under C6, with the control weight corrected to $1/(1-p(O_i))$ (also the last line of the proof in Supplement A.1.3)
canonical_claim.location: p. 759 (PDF p. 16), display defining $\hat\tau^{\mathrm{obs}}_{\mathrm{HT}}(d)$; Supplement A p. 4 (A.1.3, last line of the display)
canonical_claim.statement:
Printed. p. 759: 'Under C6 the Horvitz-Thompson estimator with known propensity scores, defined as $\hat\tau^{\mathrm{obs}}_{\mathrm{HT}}(d)=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\frac{Z_i}{p(O_i)}\mu_i(\mathbf Y;d)-\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\frac{1-Z_i}{p(O_i)}\mu_i(\mathbf Y;d)$, is unbiased for $\mathrm{AME}(d;\eta)$.' Supplement A p. 4, last line of the proof: '$=\mathrm E\Big[\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\frac{Z_i}{p(O_i)}\mu_i(\mathbf Y;d)-\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\frac{1-Z_i}{p(O_i)}\mu_i(\mathbf Y;d)\Big]$', the preceding line having the control factor $\frac{1-p(O_i)}{1-p(O_i)}$.

Corrected statement. Define $\hat\tau^{\mathrm{obs}}_{\mathrm{HT}}(d)=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\frac{Z_i}{p(O_i)}\mu_i(\mathbf Y;d)-\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\frac{1-Z_i}{1-p(O_i)}\mu_i(\mathbf Y;d)$. Under C6:
(a) $\mathrm E\big[\hat\tau^{\mathrm{obs}}_{\mathrm{HT}}(d)\big]=\mathrm{AME}(d;\eta)$, where $\eta$ is the design of independent assignments with $\Pr(Z_i=1)=p(O_i)$.
(b) The estimator as printed has expectation $\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\Big[\mu_i(1;d,\eta)-\frac{1-p(O_i)}{p(O_i)}\mu_i(0;d,\eta)\Big]$, which differs from $\mathrm{AME}(d;\eta)=\frac1N\sum_i[\mu_i(1;d,\eta)-\mu_i(0;d,\eta)]$ unless $\frac1N\sum_i\frac{1-2p(O_i)}{p(O_i)}\mu_i(0;d,\eta)=0$.
(c) Instance (validator): if $\mu_i(\mathbf Y(\mathbf z);d)=1$ for all $i$ and $\mathbf z$ and $p(O_i)=\frac14$ for all $i$, then $\mathrm{AME}(d;\eta)=0$, the printed estimator has expectation $-2$, and the corrected one has expectation $0$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: (S1)-(S3) for circle averages, $\mu_i(z_i;d,\eta)$ of (5) and the AME; C6 and footnote 19: (S7). The estimator with estimated propensities, $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{IPW}}(d)$ (Supplement A p. 14), has the control weight $1/(1-p(O_i|\hat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}}))$.
canonical_claim.note: This target is also the mathematical content of headline claim P004-H6 ('the propensity-weighted Horvitz-Thompson estimator is unbiased under C6'). Exact for each $N$: (a) and (b) follow from $\mathrm E[Z_i\mu_i(\mathbf Y;d)]=p(O_i)\mu_i(1;d,\eta)$ and $\mathrm E[(1-Z_i)\mu_i(\mathbf Y;d)]=(1-p(O_i))\mu_i(0;d,\eta)$ under independent assignment (only C6(i)-(ii) and $0<p(O_i)<1$ are used). canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 6.3, the Monte Carlo rejection rule and 'gives an $\alpha$-level exact test': (A) with a negative observed statistic the printed rule never rejects; (B) the rule with absolute values on both sides, at $P=100$ and $\alpha=\frac1{20}$, has size $0.0555>0.05$ in a sharp-null Bernoulli design with eight nodes
canonical_claim.statement:
Printed statement refuted. p. 758: 'Under the sharp null hypothesis that $Y_x(\mathbf z)=Y_x(\mathbf 0)$ for any $\mathbf z$, we know the full distribution of potential outcomes. Denote the statistic of interest as $T(\mathbf Y,\mathbf Z)$. Examples include estimates of the AMEs at each distance value or the average/maximum of such estimates on an interval $[d_1,d_2]$. As all the potential outcomes are known under the sharp null, we can resample the assignment $\mathbf z$ for $P$ times and calculate the corresponding $T(\mathbf Y,\mathbf Z_p)$, $p=1,\ldots P$. The resampling distribution of $\{T(\mathbf Y,\mathbf Z_p)\}_{p=1,\ldots P}$ will approximate the distribution of $T(\mathbf Y,\mathbf Z)$ under the sharp null. As a result, rejecting the null if $\frac1P\sum_p\mathbf 1\{|T(\mathbf Y,\mathbf Z_p)|\ge T(\mathbf Y,\mathbf Z)\}\le\alpha$ for some fixed large enough $P$ gives an $\alpha$-level exact test of the sharp null hypothesis.'

Design used in Witnesses A and B (validator; exact). Eight intervention nodes at $(3i,0)$, $i=1,\ldots,8$; one outcome point at each node, counting measure, $d=0$, so $\mu_i(\mathbf Y(\mathbf z);0)$ is the outcome at node $i$; for every $\mathbf z$, $Y_i(\mathbf z)=y_i=2^{i-1}/128$, that is $(y_1,\ldots,y_8)=(\frac1{128},\frac1{64},\frac1{32},\frac1{16},\frac18,\frac14,\frac12,1)$, so the sharp null holds; $Z_1,\ldots,Z_8$ independent Bernoulli($\frac12$) (C1 with $p=\frac12$). The statistic is the Horvitz-Thompson estimator (13) at $d=0$: $t(\mathbf z)=\frac14\sum_i(2z_i-1)y_i=\frac{2j-255}{512}$, where $j=\sum_i2^{i-1}z_i$ is uniform on $\{0,\ldots,255\}$. So $|t(\mathbf Z)|$ takes the 128 values $\frac{2r-1}{512}$, $r=1,\ldots,128$, each with probability $\frac1{128}$. The $P$ resampled assignments are i.i.d. from the same design and independent of the observed assignment.
Witness A (the missing absolute value). If $T(\mathbf Y,\mathbf Z)<0$, then $|T(\mathbf Y,\mathbf Z_p)|\ge0>T(\mathbf Y,\mathbf Z)$ for every $p$, the printed proportion equals $1$, and the rule does not reject for any $\alpha<1$. In the design above with $T=t$, the event that the observed assignment has $j=0$ ($t=-\frac{255}{512}$) and all $P=100$ resamples have $j=127$ ($t=-\frac1{512}$) has probability $256^{-101}>0$; on it the printed proportion is $1$, the proportion with $|T(\mathbf Y,\mathbf Z)|$ on the right-hand side is $0$, and the corrected p-value of target P004-T13 is $\frac1{101}$.
Witness B (the level). Take the nonnegative statistic $T=|t|$, for which the printed rule is the rule with absolute values on both sides, $P=100$ and $\alpha=\frac1{20}$. With $B=\sum_{p=1}^{100}\mathbf 1\{|t(\mathbf Z_p)|\ge|t(\mathbf Z)|\}$ the rule rejects iff $B\le5$, and its exact rejection probability under the sharp null is $s=\frac1{128^{101}}\sum_{m=1}^{128}\sum_{b=0}^5\binom{100}bm^b(128-m)^{100-b}=0.05549969550\ldots>\frac1{20}$. (With the signed statistic $T=t$ and the rule exactly as printed, the size is $s/2=0.0277\ldots$, since the 128 assignments with $t<0$ never reject.)
Witness C (a large $P$). Seventeen nodes, $y_i=2^{i-1}/2^{16}$, the same design otherwise, so $t(\mathbf z)=\frac{2j-(2^{17}-1)}{17\cdot2^{15}}$ with $j$ uniform on $\{0,\ldots,2^{17}-1\}$ and $|t|$ uniform on $M=2^{16}$ values; $P=10000$, $\alpha=\frac1{20}$, rejection iff $B\le500$. The exact size $s_M=\frac1M\sum_{m=1}^Mf(m/M)$, with $f(q)=\sum_{b=0}^{500}\binom{10000}bq^b(1-q)^{10000-b}$, satisfies $s_M\ge\int_0^1f(q)\,\mathrm dq-\frac1M=\frac{501}{10001}-\frac1{65536}=\frac{32823535}{655425536}>\frac1{20}$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Sharp null and statistic: the quoted paragraph. Horvitz-Thompson estimator (13): (S5). C1: (S4). 'Exact $\alpha$-level' is read as: rejection probability at most $\alpha$ under the sharp null, over the observed assignment and the Monte Carlo draws jointly. In Section 8.1 (p. 763) the observed statistic is $-0.034$ and the reported p-value is 'around 0.065', which the printed rule cannot give.
canonical_claim.note: All three witnesses are finite and exact. In B, given that the observed $|t|$ has upper rank $m$ among its 128 values (each $m$ has probability $\frac1{128}$), $B\sim\mathrm{Bin}(100,\frac m{128})$; the reduced fraction for $s$ is in exact_output.txt and exact_results.json in the same folder. In C, $f$ is nonincreasing with $f(0)=1$, $f(1)=0$, and $\int_0^1\binom Pbq^b(1-q)^{P-b}\mathrm dq=\frac1{P+1}$. Scope (the verdict is confirmed in part): not every finite $P$ is invalid (at $\alpha=\frac1{20}$ and $P=9999$ the rule coincides with the corrected one), and for a fixed finite design the rule is conservative for all sufficiently large $P$ (for the eight-node design, for all $P\ge8{,}000{,}000$); what is refuted is a level guarantee that holds merely because $P$ is large. The simulation code uses absolute values on both sides.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 6.3, the Monte Carlo randomization test, corrected: absolute value of the observed statistic and the observed assignment counted among the draws
canonical_claim.statement:
Printed. p. 758: 'Under the sharp null hypothesis that $Y_x(\mathbf z)=Y_x(\mathbf 0)$ for any $\mathbf z$, we know the full distribution of potential outcomes. Denote the statistic of interest as $T(\mathbf Y,\mathbf Z)$. Examples include estimates of the AMEs at each distance value or the average/maximum of such estimates on an interval $[d_1,d_2]$. As all the potential outcomes are known under the sharp null, we can resample the assignment $\mathbf z$ for $P$ times and calculate the corresponding $T(\mathbf Y,\mathbf Z_p)$, $p=1,\ldots P$. The resampling distribution of $\{T(\mathbf Y,\mathbf Z_p)\}_{p=1,\ldots P}$ will approximate the distribution of $T(\mathbf Y,\mathbf Z)$ under the sharp null. As a result, rejecting the null if $\frac1P\sum_p\mathbf 1\{|T(\mathbf Y,\mathbf Z_p)|\ge T(\mathbf Y,\mathbf Z)\}\le\alpha$ for some fixed large enough $P$ gives an $\alpha$-level exact test of the sharp null hypothesis.'

Corrected statement. Assume the sharp null hypothesis $Y_x(\mathbf z)=Y_x(\mathbf 0)$ for all $x\in\mathcal X$ and all $\mathbf z$. Let $\mathbf Z$ be the observed assignment and let $\mathbf Z^{(1)},\ldots,\mathbf Z^{(P)}$ be independent draws from the assignment law of the experiment, independent of $\mathbf Z$. Put $B=\sum_{r=1}^P\mathbf 1\{|T(\mathbf Y,\mathbf Z^{(r)})|\ge|T(\mathbf Y,\mathbf Z)|\}$ and $p_+=\frac{1+B}{P+1}$.
(a) For every integer $P\ge1$ and every $\alpha\in(0,1)$, $\mathbf{Prob}(p_+\le\alpha)\le\alpha$: rejecting when $p_+\le\alpha$ is a level-$\alpha$ test of the sharp null for every $P$, with no continuity or no-ties condition (it may be conservative).
(b) For the uncorrected rule with absolute values on both sides, $\mathbf{Prob}\big(\frac BP\le\alpha\big)\le\frac{\lfloor\alpha P\rfloor+1}{P+1}\le\alpha+\frac{1-\alpha}{P+1}$, and the first bound can exceed $\alpha$ (target P004-T12).
(c) $p_+-\frac BP=\frac{1-B/P}{P+1}\in[0,\frac1{P+1}]$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: $T(\mathbf Y,\mathbf Z)$: any real statistic of the outcomes and the assignment; under the sharp null the outcomes do not depend on the assignment, so $S_0=|T(\mathbf Y,\mathbf Z)|,S_1=|T(\mathbf Y,\mathbf Z^{(1)})|,\ldots,S_P$ are i.i.d. (hence exchangeable). No assumption on interference or on the design beyond drawing the resamples from the law of $\mathbf Z$ is needed.
canonical_claim.note: From smallest_repair and Sections 5-6 of the derivation. Proof idea for (a): with $R_i=\#\{j\in\{0,\ldots,P\}:S_j\ge S_i\}$, for any real numbers $S_0,\ldots,S_P$ and integer $k$ at most $k$ indices have $R_i\le k$; by exchangeability $(P+1)\Pr(R_0\le k)=\mathrm E[\#\{i:R_i\le k\}]\le k$; take $k=\lfloor\alpha(P+1)\rfloor$ and note $p_+=R_0/(P+1)$. (b) is the same argument with the event $R_0\le\lfloor\alpha P\rfloor+1$. Under the sharp null in the printed form ($Y_x(\mathbf z)=Y_x(\mathbf 0)$ for any $\mathbf z$; footnote 22 writes it with the node index, finding P004-N001).

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 6.2, the sentence after eq. (26): 'The donut and disk AMEs, defined in Section 3, are special cases with (properly-normalized) uniform kernels.' Finite designs in which the disk and donut AMEs differ from every common-kernel smoothing of the circle AMEs
canonical_claim.location: p. 757 (PDF p. 14), sentence after eq. (26); definitions: eq. (2), p. 747 (PDF p. 4); eqs. (4)-(9), pp. 749-750
canonical_claim.statement:
Printed statement refuted. p. 757: 'The AME at a particular distance $d$ with $\Omega_d=\{d\}$, as defined in (2), may be a noisy quantity to estimate well in practice. When the AME curve as a function of $d$ is considered to be smooth, it may be preferable to target an alternative quantity, the smoothed AME at d, defined as (26) $\mathrm{sAME}(d;\eta)=\int_{\mathbb R}\mathrm{AME}(t;\eta)K_h\Big(\frac{d-t}h\Big)dt$, where $K:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^+$ is a nonnegative kernel and $h$ is a user-specified bandwidth. The integral can be similarly defined for measures with discrete supports. This quantity is a smoothed version of the AME function, defined with respect to a chosen kernel function and the bandwidth. The donut and disk AMEs, defined in Section 3, are special cases with (properly-normalized) uniform kernels.' Formal reading: for a disk $\Omega=[0,d]$ or donut $\Omega=[d-\kappa,d]$, the AME defined through (2), (8), (9) with the set $\Omega$ equals the smoothing (26) of the singleton-circle AMEs $t\mapsto\mathrm{AME}(t;\eta)$ with a kernel that is constant on the band and suitably normalized; in the discrete-support case, a weighted average of the circle AMEs at the supported radii with equal weights (or, more generally, with weights common to all nodes).

Witness 1 (validator; exact; one node). One intervention node at $(0,0)$ with $Z_1\sim$ Bernoulli($\frac12$); $\zeta$ puts mass one on each of the outcome points $A=(1,0)$, $B=(0,2)$, $C=(-2,0)$ (Euclidean distances $1,2,2$); $Y_A(z)=0$, $Y_B(z)=Y_C(z)=z$, and outcomes are $0$ elsewhere. Then $\mathrm{AME}(\{1\};\eta)=0$, $\mathrm{AME}(\{2\};\eta)=1$, the equal-weight average over the two supported radii is $\frac12$, while the disk AME for $\Omega=[0,2]$ and the donut AME for $\Omega=[1,2]$ both equal $\frac{0+1+1}3=\frac23$. The weights that reproduce them are the normalized shell masses $(\frac13,\frac23)$.
Witness 2 (validator; exact; two nodes, no common kernel). Nodes $1=(0,0)$ and $2=(3,0)$ with independent Bernoulli($\frac12$) assignments; $\zeta$ puts mass one on $A=(0,4)$, $B=(3,4)$, $C=(3,-4)$, whose distances to node 1 are $(4,5,5)$ and to node 2 are $(5,4,4)$; $Y_x(\mathbf z)=1+z_1g_1(x)+z_2g_2(x)$ with $(g_1(A),g_1(B),g_1(C))=(0,1,1)$ and $(g_2(A),g_2(B),g_2(C))=(-1,0,0)$, and $Y_x(\mathbf z)=1$ elsewhere. Then $\tau_1(\{4\};\eta)=0$, $\tau_2(\{4\};\eta)=0$, $\tau_1(\{5\};\eta)=1$, $\tau_2(\{5\};\eta)=-1$, so $\mathrm{AME}(\{4\};\eta)=\mathrm{AME}(\{5\};\eta)=0$ and every weighted combination $w_4\mathrm{AME}(\{4\};\eta)+w_5\mathrm{AME}(\{5\};\eta)$ is $0$; but for the disk $\Omega=[0,5]$ (and for the donut $\Omega=[4,5]$), $\tau_1(\Omega;\eta)=\frac23$, $\tau_2(\Omega;\eta)=-\frac13$ and $\mathrm{AME}(\Omega;\eta)=\frac16$. The normalized shell masses are $(\frac13,\frac23)$ for node 1 and $(\frac23,\frac13)$ for node 2.
Witness 3 (validator; area measure). One point node at the origin, $\zeta$ = area on the unit disk, $Y_x(z)=z\|x\|$. The effect on the circle of radius $r$ is $r$; its average over $r\in[0,1]$ with the uniform kernel is $\int_0^1r\,\mathrm dr=\frac12$; the disk AME for $\Omega=[0,1]$ is $\frac{\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^1r\cdot r\,\mathrm dr\,\mathrm d\theta}{\pi}=\frac23$. For the annulus $\Omega=[\frac12,1]$ the uniform-radius average is $\frac34$ and the donut AME is $\frac79$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: (S2): the circle average (2) for a set of distances $\Omega_d$, the measure $\zeta$, singleton, donut and disk sets, and discrete outcome supports. (S3): marginalization (4)-(6), $\tau_i$ (8), AME (9); here $\tau_i(\Omega;\eta)$ and $\mathrm{AME}(\Omega;\eta)$ denote (8) and (9) computed with the distance set $\Omega$. In Witness 3 the effect on a circle (a set of zero area) is the conditional mean of the point effects given the distance, as in the article's own reading of a circle average.
canonical_claim.note: Witnesses 1 and 2 are finite sums over atoms and assignments; Witness 3 is two elementary integrals. The defect is in the stated identity between two estimands; no estimate, simulation or application number in the paper is derived from it. Equality can hold in special cases (for instance constant effects, or equal normalized shell masses).
